explanation: Count++ is read-modify-write, so two threads can read the same value and both write back the same incremented value, losing one update. volatile only guarantees visibility of the latest write, not atomicity of a compound action. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is atomic, and a lock would also work.
options: volatile makes count++ atomic.
The JVM reorders the loop body.
Two threads can interleave the read, increment and write of count++, losing an update.
AtomicInteger is slower, so the JVM skips updates.
prompt: A shared int counter incremented by two threads with volatile ends up below the expected total. Why?
title: Lost update with volatile

explanation: A fixed pool of 2 threads with an unbounded queue will accept tasks forever, so a burst can queue millions of tasks and exhaust memory. A bounded queue plus an explicit rejection policy (abort, caller-runs, or discard) makes overload visible and bounded. More threads alone only moves the bottleneck; shutting down the pool after submit is not a sizing fix.
options: Use a cached thread pool instead.
Increase the pool to 200 threads.
Use a bounded work queue with an explicit rejection policy, so overload is bounded and visible.
Submit tasks with invokeAll instead of submit.
prompt: A fixed pool of 2 threads with an unbounded queue runs out of memory under a burst of tasks. What is the best fix?
title: Executor queue sizing

explanation: The young generation is collected frequently and cheaply because most objects die young (the weak generational hypothesis); surviving objects are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely and more expensively. Tenuring thresholds control how many young collections an object survives before promotion.
options: Objects are allocated in the old generation first.
Most objects die young, so the young generation is collected often and cheaply, and survivors are promoted.
The young generation is never collected.
Promotion happens on every method call.
prompt: Why does the JVM split the heap into a young and an old generation?
title: Generational garbage collection

explanation: A JWT is signed, so the server can verify it without storing session state, but its claims cannot be changed after signing — the token stays valid until it expires. That is why access tokens are kept short-lived and revocation is handled by expiry plus refresh-token rotation, a denylist, or a version claim, rather than by editing the token.
options: Delete the token from the database.
You cannot edit a signed token; you must wait for expiry or use short lifetimes plus a revocation mechanism such as refresh rotation or a denylist.
Change the signing key for just that user.
Send the token a logout request.
prompt: A user's JWT must be invalidated immediately after logout. Why is this not as simple as deleting a session?
title: JWT revocation

explanation: Accessing a lazily loaded association after the persistence context (EntityManager / transaction) has closed throws LazyInitializationException, because there is no session left to fetch the data. Fetching the needed data inside the transaction with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph, or mapping to a DTO inside the transaction, fixes it. Open Session in View hides the problem by keeping the session open into the view layer, at the cost of unpredictable queries.
options: The entity has no default constructor.
The lazy association is accessed after the persistence context has closed.
The association is annotated fetch = EAGER.
The query used a DTO projection.
title: LazyInitializationException

explanation: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing downstream service after a threshold, fails fast, and periodically lets a trial call through to check recovery. Retrying immediately and forever amplifies the overload; adding threads only delays saturation; caching only helps if stale data is acceptable for that endpoint.
options: Retry every failed call immediately and indefinitely.
Increase the caller thread pool until the downstream recovers.
Trip a circuit breaker: fail fast after a failure threshold and probe periodically for recovery.
Cache every response permanently.
prompt: Service A calls a failing Service B, and retries pile up until A also collapses. Which pattern prevents this cascade?
title: Circuit breaker

options: List<? super Number>
List<Number>
List<? extends Number>
List<Object>

title: Wildcard for a producer

explanation: Buffered streams batch many small reads/writes into fewer system calls, which is the main win. try-with-resources still matters, but it closes the stream; it does not batch I/O. Files.readAllLines loads the whole file into memory, which is fine for small files but not for large ones, and NIO's Files.lines streams lazily.
options: Buffered streams compress the file.
Buffered streams batch small reads and writes into fewer system calls.
Buffered streams make files thread-safe.

title: Buffered I/O

back: Happens-before: a write to a volatile variable (or releasing a lock, or starting a thread) happens-before every subsequent read of that variable (or acquiring the same lock, or the started thread's actions). It is the guarantee that makes one thread's writes visible to another.
front: What is the happens-before relationship, in one sentence?
title: Happens-before

back: A stop-the-world pause is a period when application threads are stopped so the collector can safely reclaim memory. Long pauses hurt latency; collectors such as G1 and ZGC aim to keep pauses short and predictable, at the cost of more total CPU or memory.
front: What is a stop-the-world GC pause, and why does it matter?
title: Stop-the-world pauses

back: Access token: short-lived (minutes), sent with each request, proves identity. Refresh token: long-lived, stored securely, used only to obtain a new access token. Never put sensitive data in a JWT payload, because it is only base64-encoded, not encrypted.
front: Access token vs refresh token — and what must never go in a JWT payload?
title: Access vs refresh tokens

It prints nothing because the future never completes
title: CompletableFuture chain output

description: Two threads each transfer money between the same two accounts, but in opposite directions, and the program sometimes hangs forever. Diagnose the problem and propose a fix that preserves correctness.
solution: This is deadlock: each thread holds one account's lock and waits for the other's. Fix it by imposing a single global lock order — for example, always lock the account with the smaller id first — so no thread can hold one lock while waiting for a lock another thread holds in the opposite order. Alternatives include using one lock per transfer operation, or tryLock with a timeout and retry, but a consistent lock order is the cleanest fix. Also verify with thread dumps that the hang is a lock cycle, not an infinite loop.
title: Deadlock in account transfers

description: A latency-sensitive service suffers periodic 2-second pauses, and GC logs show long old-generation collections. How do you investigate and reduce the pauses without guessing at flags?
solution: First confirm GC is the cause: enable GC logging (for example -Xlog:gc*) and correlate pause timestamps with the latency spikes. Then check what is being promoted: look for large short-lived allocations, oversized caches, or objects surviving because of long-lived references. Reduce allocation (reuse buffers, avoid boxing in hot paths, cap caches) before tuning the collector. If pauses remain, try a low-pause collector such as G1 with a pause-time goal or ZGC, and measure throughput and pause percentiles before and after — a collector change that fixes p99 at the cost of unacceptable throughput is not a win.
title: Diagnosing long GC pauses

description: A single-page app stores a long-lived JWT in localStorage and calls APIs with it. After a token theft incident, the team must redesign token handling. What should change, and what should stay?
solution: Move to short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus rotating refresh tokens: each refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token is detected on reuse and the whole token family can be revoked. Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie rather than localStorage where JavaScript can read it, and keep the short-lived access token in memory. Never put passwords, roles that must be revocable, or other sensitive data in the JWT payload, since it is only base64-encoded. Add a server-side revocation list or token version for immediate logout of compromised accounts.
title: Redesigning JWT handling after theft

description: A controller returns a JPA entity directly. The JSON serializer touches a lazily loaded collection and the request fails with LazyInitializationException in production but not in tests. Explain the difference and propose a fix.
solution: In tests the transaction (or Open Session in View) is often still open when serialization happens, so lazy loading succeeds; in production the transaction has closed before the serializer runs. Fix it properly: fetch exactly what the response needs inside the transaction — a JOIN FETCH query, an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection — and return a DTO, not the entity. That also prevents leaking internal fields and accidental extra queries. Do not fix it by marking the association EAGER or by enabling Open Session in View in production, both of which hide the problem and cause unpredictable queries.
title: LazyInitializationException in production only

description: Checkout calls inventory, payment and notification services in sequence. When payment is slow, checkout threads block, timeouts cascade, and one slow service takes down the whole checkout flow. Propose a resilient design using timeouts, bulkheads and observability.
solution: Give every downstream call an explicit timeout (shorter than the caller's own timeout) so a slow service fails fast instead of holding threads. Isolate each dependency with a bulkhead — a dedicated thread pool or concurrency limit — so payment slowness cannot exhaust the pool used for inventory. Add a circuit breaker so repeated failures fail fast and recover gradually, and retry only idempotent calls with backoff and a cap. Make payment calls idempotent with an idempotency key so a retried request cannot double-charge. Expose health, metrics and traces (via Actuator and distributed tracing) so the slow dependency is visible before it cascades, and design the checkout to degrade gracefully — for example, queue the notification instead of blocking checkout on it.
title: Resilient checkout across microservices
